title: How To Save Yourself A Mountain Of Stress And Misbehavior and-misbehavior/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin explains why small, seemingly minor misbehaviors in September inevitably snowball into major disruptions later in the year if left unaddressed. He identifies two common teacher failure patterns: inconsistently enforcing a classroom management plan (letting severity, mood, or the student involved determine whether a consequence is given), and never clearly defining behavior expectations in the first place. Both approaches, he argues, breed distrust, confusion, and a sense of unfairness that students sense acutely, prompting them to test limits and push back. The remedy is to thoroughly and specifically teach expectations from the very start of the year and then hold students to them with total consistency, which he frames as the foundation of a peaceful classroom through June.
points: Small, unaddressed behaviors in September compound over the year—by November they disrupt lessons, and by March they affect the teacher's health.
Inconsistent enforcement of a classroom management plan (based on mood, severity, or student identity) breeds distrust and a sense of unfairness.
Failing to clearly and thoroughly define behavior expectations up front ('I'll know it when I see it') is even more common and equally damaging.
Unclear expectations make it impossible to recognize a problem before it's too late, and lead to student pushback and disrespect when finally addressed.
The fix is to thoroughly teach expectations 'from A to Z' at the start of the year and hold students to them 100% of the time thereafter.
quotes: Small, seemingly insignificant behaviors in September will in almost every circumstance multiply into major disruptions down the road.
Well, one of the truisms of classroom management is that little things don’t stay little for long.
Inconsistency communicates to students that you don’t mean what you say and therefore can’t be trusted.
The second common approach that leads to growing and pervading misbehavior is when teachers are unclear about what they expect from students. This is the “I’ll know it when I see it” approach.
The lesson here is that you can’t effectively hold students accountable for that which hasn’t been clearly and thoroughly defined for them.

The solution to both faulty approaches is to take the time to thoroughly teach what you expect from your students, from A to Z and back again, based on the clarity of what you want each day to look like.
